## Chapter Summary

An analysis that supports a decision or an audit conclusion must be accurate and reviewable, and the structure of the workbook that holds it is one of the controls that make it so. Research on operational spreadsheets finds errors in a small percentage of cells, which in a large workbook makes some errors close to certain, and it finds that the quality control around spreadsheets is usually informal. Structured design practices remove common opportunities for error and make the remaining logic visible to a reviewer, although they do not replace careful review.

Excel Tables manage a dataset as a single named object that knows its own extent. Structured references, such as `SalesInvoiceLine[LineTotal]` and `[@Quantity]`, refer to Table data by name, so formulas remain correct as the data grows and state their own logic to a reviewer. Calculated columns apply one formula to every row of a Table. Power Query brings data into a workbook without altering its source: it connects to a file such as CharlesRiver.xlsx, records every filter and change as an applied step, loads the result as a Table named after the query, and repeats all of it on refresh. The analysis workbook you built imports only the Tables and rows the Furniture question needs, and its control totals prove that the import is complete.

Relative, absolute, and mixed references determine how a formula changes when it is copied. Relative references suit row-by-row calculations, absolute references point every copy at one cell, and mixed references let a single formula fill a two-way grid. Structured references stay fixed when copied but shift when filled across, which is a trap worth remembering. Named cells hold the parameters of an analysis, such as a threshold derived from the data with PERCENTILE.INC, and make every formula that uses them easier to read.

Multi-level sorts, condition-based filters, and slicers let you explore transaction data one question at a time, and the SUBTOTAL function summarizes only the rows in view. Conditional formatting, including formula-based rules that shade whole rows, makes patterns and exceptions visible, and data validation protects parameter cells from implausible entries. A layered workbook, with data, parameters, analysis, and a documentation worksheet placed first, lets a reviewer follow any number back to its source. Applied to the Charles River invoice lines, these tools showed that the Furniture Seasonal Promotion accounts for more promotion lines and more discount dollars than any other promotion, a clue to the controller's question that the rest of Part II will test.
